reminder: An equilateral [triangle](c:triangle) has three sides of equal length and three angles of $60^\circ$.
definition: A [triangle](c:triangle) is equilateral when its three sides have the same length. Then its three [angles](c:angle) are equal too, and each one measures $60^\circ$.
examples: The triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$ and $(1/2,\sqrt3/2)$ has three sides of length $1$.
Each face of a regular tetrahedron and each face of a regular octahedron is an equilateral triangle.
Non-example: a triangle with sides $2$, $2$ and $3$ has two equal sides, but the third side differs, so it is not equilateral.

steps: Let $T$ be an equilateral triangle with side length $s$.
All sides of $T$ are equal by definition, and all angles are equal to $60^\circ$.
A [regular polygon](c:regular-polygon) is a polygon with all sides equal and all angles equal.
So $T$ is the regular polygon with three sides.
links.why: It shows that facts about regular polygons, such as the center and the circumscribed circle, also hold for equilateral triangles.

reminder: A Jordan algebra is a commutative algebra whose product satisfies the Jordan identity $(xy)(xx)=x(y(xx))$.
definition: Let $k$ be a [field](c:field) of characteristic not $2$. A Jordan algebra over $k$ is an [algebra](c:algebra-over-a-field) $J$ over $k$ whose product is commutative and satisfies $(xy)(xx)=x(y(xx))$ for all $x,y\in J$. The product does not need to be [associative](c:associative-operation).
examples: Every associative algebra $A$ gives a Jordan algebra $A^+$ with the product $x\circ y=\tfrac12(xy+yx)$.
The real symmetric $n\times n$ matrices with the product $x\circ y=\tfrac12(xy+yx)$ form a Jordan algebra.
The $3\times3$ Hermitian matrices over the octonions form a $27$-dimensional Jordan algebra that does not come from an associative algebra.
Non-example: the $2\times2$ real matrices with the ordinary matrix product are not commutative, so they are not a Jordan algebra with that product.

steps: Let $J$ be a Jordan algebra over $k$.
Its product is bilinear, so $J$ is an algebra in which associativity is not required.
A Jordan algebra adds two conditions: the product is commutative, and it satisfies the Jordan identity.
links.why: It shows that general results on nonassociative algebras apply to every Jordan algebra.

steps: Take the $3\times3$ Hermitian matrices with entries in the octonions.
Give them the product $x\circ y=\tfrac12(xy+yx)$.
This product is commutative and satisfies the Jordan identity, so the result is a Jordan algebra.
This special Jordan algebra is the [Albert algebra](c:albert-algebra), of dimension $27$ over the reals.
links.why: It shows that the Albert algebra is the standard exceptional example inside the class of Jordan algebras.

steps: Start with a real Jordan algebra $J$.
Add a complete norm on $J$ that satisfies $\|x\circ y\|\le\|x\|\,\|y\|$.
Then $J$ is a [Jordan-Banach algebra](c:jordan-banach-algebra).
links.why: It shows that a Jordan-Banach algebra is a Jordan algebra with a compatible complete norm.

reminder: The 3-sphere is the set of points at distance $1$ from the origin in $\mathbb{R}^4$.
definition: The 3-sphere $S^3$ is the unit [sphere](c:sphere) $\{x\in\mathbb{R}^4:\|x\|=1\}$, a compact smooth [manifold](c:manifold) of dimension $3$. It is also the set of unit [quaternions](c:quaternion), and as a manifold it is the [special unitary group](c:special-unitary-group) $SU(2)$.
examples: The unit quaternions $a+bi+cj+dk$ with $a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2=1$ form $S^3$.
The one-point compactification of $\mathbb{R}^3$ is $S^3$.
The Hopf map sends $S^3\subset\mathbb{C}^2$ onto the $2$-sphere, and each fibre is a circle.
Non-example: the unit sphere in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is the $2$-sphere $S^2$, a surface, so it is not the 3-sphere.

steps: The $n$-[sphere](c:sphere) is the set $S^n=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n+1}:\|x\|=1\}$.
Take $n=3$ in this definition.
The result is the set of unit vectors of $\mathbb{R}^4$, which is $S^3$.
links.why: It shows that general facts about spheres apply to $S^3$ when you put $n=3$.

steps: A [homology sphere](c:homology-sphere) is a manifold with the homology groups of a sphere.
The 3-sphere has $H_0=H_3=\mathbb{Z}$ and all other homology groups zero.
So $S^3$ is a homology sphere, and the simplest one.
links.why: It shows that the 3-sphere is the model that all homology 3-spheres imitate.

reminder: A convex curve is a closed curve in the plane that bounds a convex region.
definition: A convex curve is the boundary of a compact [convex set](c:convex-set) with interior points in the plane, that is, of a plane [convex body](c:convex-body). Equivalently, it is a [simple closed curve](c:simple-closed-curve) such that through each of its points passes a line with the whole curve on one side.
examples: A circle or an ellipse is a convex curve.
The boundary of a convex polygon, such as a square, is a convex curve with corners.
Non-example: the boundary of a crescent moon is a simple closed curve but not convex, because the segment between its two tips leaves the region.

steps: A convex curve bounds a compact convex set $K$ with interior points.
Radial projection from an interior point maps $K$ homeomorphically onto a closed disc.
So the boundary of $K$ is homeomorphic to a circle, which is a [simple closed curve](c:simple-closed-curve).
The convex case adds that the region inside the curve is convex.
links.why: It shows that every theorem about simple closed curves holds for convex curves, which add convexity.

steps: Start with a convex curve $C$ that bounds a convex body $K$.
Measure the width of $K$ in a direction as the distance between the two parallel supporting lines.
Add the condition that this width has the same value in every direction.
Then $C$ is a [curve of constant width](c:curve-of-constant-width).
links.why: It shows that constant width is one extra condition on a convex curve.

reminder: A cusp is a singular point of a curve where the curve is locally like $y^2=x^3$.
definition: An ordinary cusp of a plane [algebraic curve](c:algebraic-curve) is a [singular point](c:singular-point-of-a-curve) at which, in suitable local coordinates, the curve is $y^2=x^3$. It has one branch, $t\mapsto(t^2,t^3)$, with a sharp tip. In the theory of modular curves, a cusp is also a point at infinity of the quotient of the [upper half-plane](c:upper-half-plane) by a discrete group.
examples: The curve $y^2=x^3$ has a cusp at the origin.
The cuspidal cubic is the Weierstrass cubic $y^2=x^3$, which has its only singular point at the origin.
The modular curve $X_0(N)$ has finitely many cusps, and the curve for $\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ has one cusp.
Non-example: the curve $y^2=x^3+x^2$ has a node at the origin, with two branches and two tangent lines, so that point is not a cusp.

steps: Let $p$ be a cusp of a curve $C$, with local equation $y^2=x^3$.
The partial derivatives of $y^2-x^3$ are $2y$ and $-3x^2$, and both vanish at the origin.
So the curve is not smooth at $p$, and $p$ is a [singular point](c:singular-point-of-a-curve).
The cusp case adds that there is one branch with a single tangent line.
links.why: It shows that a cusp is the simplest singular point with one branch.

reminder: An equilibrium is Lyapunov stable when solutions that start close to it stay close to it for all later time.
definition: Let $x^*$ be an equilibrium of the [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) $\dot x=f(x)$, so $f(x^*)=0$. The equilibrium is Lyapunov stable when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that every solution with $\|x(0)-x^*\|<\delta$ satisfies $\|x(t)-x^*\|<\varepsilon$ for all $t\ge0$.
examples: The origin is Lyapunov stable for $\dot x=-x$, because $|x(t)|=|x(0)|e^{-t}$ never grows.
The origin is Lyapunov stable for the oscillator $\ddot x=-x$, although solutions never converge to it.
Non-example: the origin is not stable for $\dot x=x$, because every solution with $x(0)\ne0$ leaves each small ball.

steps: Start with a Lyapunov stable equilibrium $x^*$.
Add the condition that every solution of the system converges to $x^*$ as $t\to\infty$.
Then $x^*$ is globally asymptotically stable.
links.why: It shows that global asymptotic stability is stability plus global attraction.

reminder: A strong subtree keeps, for each of its nodes, one extension above every immediate successor, and it skips whole levels.
definition: Let $T$ be a [rooted tree](c:rooted-tree) of height $\omega$ in which every node has finitely many immediate successors. A strong subtree of $T$ is a subset $S\subseteq T$ with levels $l_0<l_1<\cdots$ of $T$ such that the $n$th level of $S$ lies in level $l_n$ of $T$. Each node $s\in S$ at level $l_n$ has, above each immediate successor $t$ of $s$ in $T$, exactly one node of $S$ at level $l_{n+1}$, and these nodes are the immediate successors of $s$ in $S$.
examples: In the tree $2^{<\omega}$ of finite $0$-$1$ strings, the strings of even length whose bits at odd positions are all $0$ form a strong subtree with levels $0,2,4,\dots$.
Every tree $T$ of the kind above is a strong subtree of itself, with $l_n=n$.
Non-example: in $2^{<\omega}$ the branch $\{0^n:n\in\mathbb{N}\}$ is not a strong subtree, because above the successor $0^n1$ of $0^n$ it keeps no node.

reminder: A closed positive current is a current that vanishes on exact forms and takes nonnegative values on positive test forms.
definition: Let $X$ be a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) of dimension $n$. A closed positive current of bidimension $(p,p)$ on $X$ is a [current](c:current-distribution-theory) $T$ with $dT=0$, that is $T(d\eta)=0$ for all test forms $\eta$, and with $T(\varphi)\ge0$ for every positive test form $\varphi$ of bidegree $(p,p)$. Such forms are the sums of $f\,i\alpha_1\wedge\bar\alpha_1\wedge\cdots\wedge i\alpha_p\wedge\bar\alpha_p$ with $f\ge0$ and $\alpha_j$ of type $(1,0)$.
examples: For a closed complex submanifold $Z\subseteq X$ of dimension $p$, integration over $Z$ is a closed positive current of bidimension $(p,p)$.
The Kähler form $\omega$ of a Kähler manifold gives the closed positive current $\varphi\mapsto\int\omega\wedge\varphi$.
If $u$ is a plurisubharmonic function, then $dd^cu$ is a closed positive $(1,1)$-current.
Non-example: $-[Z]$, minus the integration current of a complex hypersurface, is closed but not positive.

steps: A [current](c:current-distribution-theory) is a continuous linear functional on compactly supported smooth differential forms.
A closed positive current is such a functional.
It adds two conditions: it vanishes on exact forms $d\eta$, and it is nonnegative on positive test forms.
links.why: It shows that closed positive currents are currents with two extra conditions, so general facts about currents apply.

reminder: A distributive law lets two monads on one category combine, by a natural transformation that respects both units and both multiplications.
definition: A distributive law of a [monad](c:monad) $S$ over a monad $T$ on a [category](c:category) is a [natural transformation](c:natural-transformation) $\lambda:ST\Rightarrow TS$ that is compatible with the units and the multiplications of both monads. It makes $TS$ a monad, and it lifts $T$ to a monad on the [algebras](c:algebra-over-a-monad) of $S$.
examples: Let $S$ be the free monoid monad and $T$ the free abelian group monad. The map that multiplies out a list of formal sums into a formal sum of lists is a distributive law, and $TS$ is the free ring monad.
Replace the free abelian group monad by the free commutative monoid monad to get the free semiring monad.
Non-example: there is no distributive law of the powerset monad over itself, so the composite of the powerset functor with itself is not a monad in this way.

steps: Take two monads $S$ and $T$ on the same category.
A distributive law is a [natural transformation](c:natural-transformation) $\lambda:ST\Rightarrow TS$ between the two composite functors.
It adds four conditions: $\lambda$ respects the two units and the two multiplications.
links.why: It shows that a distributive law is a natural transformation with four coherence conditions.

reminder: A domino tiling covers a region of unit squares with dominoes, so that no square is left bare or covered twice.
definition: A domino tiling of a region $R$ made of unit squares is a set of dominoes, each formed by two squares that share a side, such that every square of $R$ lies in exactly one domino. Equivalently, it is a [perfect matching](c:perfect-matching) of the [graph](c:graph) whose vertices are the squares of $R$ and whose edges join squares that share a side.
examples: A $2\times3$ rectangle has exactly $3$ domino tilings, and a $2\times n$ rectangle has a Fibonacci number of them.
The $8\times8$ chessboard has $12988816$ domino tilings.
Non-example: the $8\times8$ chessboard with two opposite corners removed has no domino tiling, because it has $32$ squares of one colour and $30$ of the other, and each domino covers one of each.

steps: Let $R$ be a region of unit squares, and let $G_R$ be the graph with one vertex per square and one edge per pair of squares that share a side.
A domino covers two adjacent squares, so it is an edge of $G_R$.
A tiling covers each square exactly once, so its dominoes are edges that meet every vertex exactly once.
Such a set of edges is a [perfect matching](c:perfect-matching) of $G_R$, and here $G_R$ is a bipartite grid graph.
links.why: It shows that counting domino tilings is counting perfect matchings of a grid graph.

reminder: The fixed-point index of an isolated fixed point is the degree of the direction of $x-f(x)$ on a small sphere around it.
definition: Let $f:U\to\mathbb{R}^n$ be a [continuous map](c:continuous-function) on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $p$ be an isolated [fixed point](c:fixed-point) of $f$. The fixed-point index of $f$ at $p$ is the [degree](c:degree-of-a-map) of the map $z\mapsto(z-f(z))/\|z-f(z)\|$ from a small sphere around $p$ to the unit sphere. If $f$ is differentiable at $p$ and $I-Df(p)$ is invertible, the index is the sign of $\det(I-Df(p))$.
examples: The map $f(x)=x/2$ on $\mathbb{R}$ has index $+1$ at $0$, because $1-\tfrac12>0$.
The map $f(x)=2x$ on $\mathbb{R}$ has index $-1$ at $0$, because $1-2<0$.
A rotation of the plane by an angle $\theta\ne0$ has index $+1$ at the origin, because $\det(I-R)=2-2\cos\theta>0$.
Non-example: the identity of $\mathbb{R}^n$ fixes every point, so no fixed point is isolated and the index at one point is not defined.

steps: Choose a small sphere $S$ around the isolated fixed point $p$ that contains no other fixed point.
On $S$ the vector $z-f(z)$ is never zero, so $z\mapsto(z-f(z))/\|z-f(z)\|$ is a map from $S$ to the unit sphere.
The [degree](c:degree-of-a-map) of this particular map is the fixed-point index at $p$.
links.why: It shows that the index is an ordinary degree, so degree theory computes it.

reminder: A homothety multiplies the vector from a fixed center to every point by the same nonzero factor.
definition: A homothety of a [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) with center $c$ and ratio $k\ne0$ is the map $h(x)=c+k(x-c)$. It fixes $c$, sends every line through $c$ to itself, and multiplies every distance by $|k|$.
examples: The map $x\mapsto2x$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is a homothety with center $0$ and ratio $2$.
The map $x\mapsto-x$ is the homothety with center $0$ and ratio $-1$, the point reflection.
The map $x\mapsto3x+1$ of $\mathbb{R}$ is a homothety with center $-\tfrac12$ and ratio $3$.
Non-example: the stretch $(x,y)\mapsto(2x,y)$ scales by $2$ in one direction and by $1$ in the other, so it is not a homothety.

steps: Let $h$ be a homothety with center $c$ and ratio $k$.
Then $h(x)-h(y)=k(x-y)$ for all points $x$ and $y$.
So $\|h(x)-h(y)\|=|k|\,\|x-y\|$, and $h$ multiplies every distance by the same constant.
A map with this property is a [similarity transformation](c:similarity-transformation), and the homothety also fixes a center.
links.why: It shows that a homothety is the similarity that keeps every line through the center in place.

steps: Write the homothety as $h(x)=kx+(1-k)c$.
This is the linear map $x\mapsto kx$ followed by a translation by $(1-k)c$.
So $h$ is an [affine map](c:affine-map), and the homothety case adds that the linear part is the scalar $k$.
links.why: It shows that homotheties are the affine maps whose linear part is a scalar.

reminder: An indexed category gives a category for each object of a base category, with reindexing functors along its morphisms.
definition: An indexed category over a base [category](c:category) $\mathcal{S}$ is a [pseudofunctor](c:pseudofunctor) $\mathbb{C}:\mathcal{S}^{op}\to\mathrm{Cat}$. It gives a category $\mathbb{C}^I$ for each object $I$ and a reindexing [functor](c:functor) $f^*:\mathbb{C}^J\to\mathbb{C}^I$ for each morphism $f:I\to J$, with coherent isomorphisms $(gf)^*\cong f^*g^*$ and $1^*\cong1$.
examples: Over the category of sets, $I\mapsto\mathcal{C}^I$ sends a set $I$ to the category of $I$-indexed families of objects of $\mathcal{C}$, and $f^*$ is precomposition with $f$.
For a category $\mathcal{S}$ with pullbacks, $I\mapsto\mathcal{S}/I$ with $f^*$ given by pullback along $f$ is an indexed category, the self-indexing of $\mathcal{S}$.
Non-example: a family of categories $(\mathcal{C}_I)_I$ with no reindexing functors along morphisms $f:I\to J$ is only a list of categories, not an indexed category.

steps: Fix a base category $\mathcal{S}$ and take the opposite category $\mathcal{S}^{op}$ as the source.
Take the 2-category $\mathrm{Cat}$ of categories as the target.
A [pseudofunctor](c:pseudofunctor) from $\mathcal{S}^{op}$ to $\mathrm{Cat}$ is exactly an indexed category.
links.why: It shows that indexed categories are pseudofunctors into $\mathrm{Cat}$, so the rules for pseudofunctors apply.

steps: Start with a [presheaf](c:presheaf) $F:\mathcal{S}^{op}\to\mathrm{Set}$.
Regard each set $F(I)$ as a discrete category, which has only identity morphisms.
The restriction maps become reindexing functors, and the coherence isomorphisms are identities.
So $F$ is an indexed category with discrete fibres.
links.why: It shows that indexed categories extend presheaves by letting each fibre be a category.

reminder: A closed Jacobi diagram is a connected graph of trivalent vertices that contains an oriented circle.
definition: A closed Jacobi diagram is a connected undirected [graph](c:graph) that contains an embedded oriented [circle](c:circle) and in which every vertex is trivalent. Each vertex carries an orientation, that is a cyclic order of its three edges, and diagrams are taken up to cyclic relabelling of the circle.
examples: A circle with one chord is a Jacobi diagram: the chord joins two trivalent vertices on the circle.
A circle with three chords that meet at one internal trivalent vertex, the tripod, is a Jacobi diagram.
Non-example: a circle with two chords that cross at a common four-valent vertex is not a Jacobi diagram, because every vertex must be trivalent.

steps: Start with a [chord diagram](c:chord-diagram), a circle with chords whose endpoints are distinct points of the circle.
Each endpoint of a chord is a trivalent vertex of the resulting graph.
So a chord diagram is a Jacobi diagram that has no internal vertices.
links.why: It shows that Jacobi diagrams extend chord diagrams by allowing internal trivalent vertices.

steps: A Jacobi diagram has vertices and edges, so it is a [graph](c:graph).
It adds three conditions: the graph is connected, all vertices are trivalent, and an oriented circle is embedded in it.
It also adds a cyclic order of the edges at each vertex.
links.why: It shows that a Jacobi diagram is a graph with a circle and vertex orientations.

reminder: The Monge point of a tetrahedron is the reflection of its circumcenter in its centroid.
definition: Let $s$ be a [simplex](c:simplex) of dimension $d\ge2$ in Euclidean space, with [circumcenter](c:circumcenter) $O$ and [centroid](c:centroid) $G$. Its Monge point is $M=O+\frac{d+1}{d-1}(G-O)$. For a tetrahedron, $M=2G-O$ is the common point of the six planes that each pass through the [midpoint](c:midpoint) of one edge and are perpendicular to the opposite edge.
examples: In a triangle ($d=2$) the Monge point is the orthocenter, since $M=O+3(G-O)$.
In a regular tetrahedron the circumcenter, the centroid and the Monge point all coincide.
Non-example: the centroid of a tetrahedron is not its Monge point unless it equals the circumcenter, because $M-O=2(G-O)$.

reminder: A monoid homomorphism is a map that preserves the product and sends the identity element to the identity element.
definition: A homomorphism from a [monoid](c:monoid) $M$ to a monoid $N$ is a [function](c:function) $f:M\to N$ with $f(xy)=f(x)f(y)$ for all $x,y\in M$ and $f(1)=1$. In other words, it preserves the product and the [identity element](c:identity-element).
examples: The exponential $\exp:(\mathbb{R},+)\to(\mathbb{R}_{>0},\cdot)$ is a monoid homomorphism.
The length of a word is a monoid homomorphism from the free monoid on an alphabet to $(\mathbb{N},+)$.
Non-example: the map $x\mapsto0$ from $(\mathbb{R},\cdot)$ to itself satisfies $f(xy)=f(x)f(y)$, but it sends $1$ to $0$, so it is not a monoid homomorphism.

steps: A [homomorphism](c:homomorphism) is a map between algebraic structures that preserves their operations.
A monoid has two operations: the product and the identity element.
A monoid homomorphism preserves both, so it is the homomorphism for the structure of a monoid.
links.why: It shows that monoid homomorphisms are the homomorphisms of one kind of algebraic structure.

steps: Let $f:G\to H$ be a monoid homomorphism between two groups.
So $f$ also preserves inverses, and it is a [group homomorphism](c:group-homomorphism).
links.why: It shows that a group homomorphism needs no extra check for inverses.

reminder: A finite group is $p$-stable when an element that acts quadratically on a $p$-subgroup acts, modulo the centralizer, inside the largest normal $p$-subgroup.
definition: Let $p$ be an odd prime and let $G$ be a [finite group](c:finite-group). Then $G$ is $p$-stable when for every $p$-subgroup $P$ of $G$ and every $x\in N_G(P)$ with $[P,x,x]=1$, the coset $xC_G(P)$ lies in $O_p(N_G(P)/C_G(P))$. Here $N_G(P)$ is the [normalizer](c:normalizer) of $P$, $C_G(P)$ its centralizer, and $O_p$ the largest [normal](c:normal-subgroup) $p$-subgroup of the [quotient group](c:quotient-group).
examples: Every finite $p$-group is $p$-stable, because each $N_G(P)/C_G(P)$ is again a $p$-group and equals its own $O_p$.
Every finite group of order prime to $p$ is $p$-stable, because its only $p$-subgroup is the trivial group.

Non-example: for $p=3$ the group $G=\mathbb{F}_3^2\rtimes SL_2(3)$ is not $3$-stable. Take $P=\mathbb{F}_3^2$ and $x=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$. Then $[P,x,x]=1$, but $O_3(N_G(P)/C_G(P))=O_3(SL_2(3))=1$ does not contain $xC_G(P)$.

steps: A $p$-stable group is a [finite group](c:finite-group) $G$, with $p$ an odd prime.
It adds a condition on every $p$-subgroup $P$ and every element $x$ of $N_G(P)$ with $[P,x,x]=1$.
The condition is that $xC_G(P)$ lies in $O_p(N_G(P)/C_G(P))$.
links.why: It shows that $p$-stability is a property of finite groups, which holds for some and fails for others.

reminder: A polycategory has morphisms with a finite list of objects as domain and another as codomain, composed by cutting one object.
definition: A polycategory has objects and polymorphisms $f:\Gamma\to\Delta$, where $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ are finite lists of objects, together with identities $1_A:A\to A$. Composition cuts exactly one object: it joins $f:\Gamma\to\Delta,A$ and $g:A,\Gamma'\to\Delta'$ into a morphism $\Gamma,\Gamma'\to\Delta,\Delta'$. Composition is associative and unital, compatible with permuting the lists in the symmetric case, and subject to a condition that forbids loops.
examples: Every [category](c:category) is a polycategory in which every domain list and every codomain list has length one.
Every [multicategory](c:multicategory) is a polycategory in which every codomain list has length one.
The proofs of classical linear logic, as sequents $\Gamma\vdash\Delta$ composed by cut, form a polycategory.
Non-example: a structure whose composition cuts several objects at once is not a polycategory, because polycategory composition cuts exactly one object.

steps: Start with a [multicategory](c:multicategory), whose morphisms $\Gamma\to A$ have a list as domain and one object as codomain.
Read the single codomain object $A$ as a list of length one.
Multicategory composition then cuts one object of a domain list against a codomain list of length one.
So a multicategory is a polycategory whose codomain lists all have length one.
links.why: It shows that polycategories add the freedom of several outputs to multicategories.

steps: Start with a [category](c:category).
Read each morphism $A\to B$ as a polymorphism between two lists of length one.
Composition of morphisms is then the cut of the single codomain object against the single domain object.
links.why: It shows that ordinary categories are the polycategories with only single inputs and outputs.

reminder: A stable homotopy type is a sequence of pointed homotopy types in which each one is the loop space of the next.
definition: A stable homotopy type, or spectrum, is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\ge0}$ of pointed [homotopy types](c:homotopy-type) with equivalences $E_n\simeq\Omega E_{n+1}$, where $\Omega$ is the [loop space](c:loop-space-object). Equivalently, it is an object of the stabilization of the pointed homotopy types, in which looping and [suspension](c:suspension-object) are inverse equivalences.
examples: The sphere spectrum has $E_n=\operatorname{colim}_k\Omega^k\Sigma^kS^n$.
For an abelian group $A$, the Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum $HA$ has $E_n=K(A,n)$.
Non-example: the pointed space $S^2$ is not a stable homotopy type, because $\Omega\Sigma S^2=\Omega S^3$ has homology in every even degree while $S^2$ does not.

steps: Start with the pointed spheres $S^n$.
Set $E_n=\operatorname{colim}_k\Omega^k\Sigma^kS^n$.
Then $\Omega E_{n+1}\simeq E_n$, so $(E_n)$ is a stable homotopy type.
This stable homotopy type is the [sphere spectrum](c:sphere-spectrum).
links.why: It shows that the sphere spectrum is the basic example of a stable homotopy type.

steps: Fix an abelian group $A$.
Take the Eilenberg-MacLane spaces $E_n=K(A,n)$.
The equivalences $K(A,n)\simeq\Omega K(A,n+1)$ make $(E_n)$ a stable homotopy type.
This stable homotopy type is the [Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum](c:eilenberg-maclane-spectrum) of $A$.
links.why: It shows that ordinary cohomology is represented by a stable homotopy type.

reminder: The Teichmüller space of a surface is the space of marked complex structures on the surface, up to isotopy.
definition: Let $S$ be a closed oriented surface of genus $g\ge2$. Its Teichmüller space $T(S)$ is the set of classes of pairs $(X,f)$, where $X$ is a [Riemann surface](c:riemann-surface) and $f:S\to X$ is an orientation-preserving [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) called a marking, and two pairs $(X,f)$ and $(Y,h)$ are identified when $h\circ f^{-1}$ is isotopic to a biholomorphic map. The [mapping class group](c:mapping-class-group) of $S$ acts on $T(S)$, and the quotient is the [moduli space](c:moduli-space) of Riemann surfaces of genus $g$.
examples: For genus $g\ge2$, the Teichmüller space is homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^{6g-6}$.
For the torus, the Teichmüller space is the upper half-plane, where $\tau$ marks the lattice $\mathbb{Z}+\tau\mathbb{Z}$.
Non-example: the moduli space of genus $g$ surfaces is the quotient of $T(S)$ by the mapping class group, so it forgets the marking and is not Teichmüller space.

reminder: A topos is a category that has finite limits, is cartesian closed, and has a subobject classifier.
definition: An elementary topos is a [category](c:category) $\mathcal{E}$ that has all finite [limits](c:limit-category-theory), is [cartesian closed](c:cartesian-closed-category), and has a [subobject classifier](c:classifier). The last condition says that an object $\Omega$ has a map $\top:1\to\Omega$ such that every [monomorphism](c:mono) $U\to A$ is the pullback of $\top$ along a unique map $A\to\Omega$.
examples: The category of sets is a topos, with $\Omega=\{0,1\}$, and so is the category of finite sets.
For every small category $\mathcal{C}$, the category of presheaves of sets on $\mathcal{C}$ is a topos.
The category of sheaves of sets on a topological space is a topos.
Non-example: the category of abelian groups is not a topos, because it has a zero object, and a cartesian closed category with a zero object is trivial.

steps: Let $\mathcal{E}$ be a topos.
By definition, $\mathcal{E}$ has finite products and exponential objects, so it is a [cartesian closed category](c:cartesian-closed-category).
The topos case adds all finite limits and a subobject classifier.
links.why: It shows that every topos has function objects, so one can compute with internal functions.

steps: Start with a [Grothendieck topos](c:grothendieck-topos) $\mathcal{E}$, the category of sheaves of sets on a site.
It has all finite limits and is cartesian closed.
It has a subobject classifier: the sheaf of closed sieves.
So $\mathcal{E}$ meets the three conditions and is an elementary topos.
links.why: It shows that every Grothendieck topos is an elementary topos, so general topos theory applies to sheaves.

reminder: The Weyl tensor is the trace-free part of the Riemann curvature tensor, and it measures the failure of conformal flatness.
definition: On a [pseudo-Riemannian manifold](c:pseudo-riemannian-manifold) $(M,g)$ of dimension $n\ge3$, the Weyl tensor is $C=R-P\owedge g$. Here $R$ is the [Riemann curvature](c:riemann-curvature) tensor, $\owedge$ is the Kulkarni-Nomizu product, and $P=\frac{1}{n-2}\bigl(\mathrm{Ric}-\frac{s}{2(n-1)}g\bigr)$ is built from the [Ricci curvature](c:ricci-curvature) $\mathrm{Ric}$ and the scalar curvature $s$. The tensor $C$ has the symmetries of $R$, all its traces vanish, and it does not change when $g$ is replaced by $e^{2f}g$, as a $(1,3)$-tensor.
examples: In dimension $3$ the Weyl tensor is always zero.
The Weyl tensor of a metric of constant curvature, such as the round sphere, is zero.
The Schwarzschild metric has $\mathrm{Ric}=0$, so its Weyl tensor equals its Riemann tensor and is not zero.
Non-example: the Ricci tensor is not the Weyl tensor, because it is a trace of the Riemann tensor, while all traces of the Weyl tensor vanish.

reminder: A $6j$ symbol is a matrix entry of the associator of a fusion category, taken in a basis of fusion channels.
definition: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a multiplicity-free [fusion category](c:fusion-category) and let $a,b,c,d,e,f$ be simple objects. The $6j$ symbol $F^{abc}_{d;ef}$ is the entry of the [associator](c:associator) $(a\otimes b)\otimes c\to a\otimes(b\otimes c)$ that relates two bases of $\mathrm{Hom}(d,a\otimes b\otimes c)$, one through the intermediate object $e$ in $a\otimes b$ and one through $f$ in $b\otimes c$. Together with the [fusion ring](c:fusion-ring), these numbers determine $\mathcal{C}$ up to equivalence.
examples: For the category of $G$-graded vector spaces with a $3$-cocycle $\omega$, the only nonzero $6j$ symbols are the values $\omega(g,h,k)$.

For the Fibonacci category, with simple objects $1$ and $\tau$ and $\tau\otimes\tau=1\oplus\tau$, the only nontrivial $6j$ symbols form the matrix $F^{\tau\tau\tau}_{\tau}=\begin{pmatrix}\varphi^{-1}&\varphi^{-1/2}\\\varphi^{-1/2}&-\varphi^{-1}\end{pmatrix}$, where $\varphi$ is the golden ratio.
For representations of $SU(2)$, the $6j$ symbols are the Racah-Wigner coefficients, up to normalization.
Non-example: a [Clebsch-Gordan coefficient](c:clebsch-gordan-coefficient) records one fusion vertex, not a change of bracketing, so it is not a $6j$ symbol.

reminder: An alternative ring is a nonassociative ring whose associator vanishes whenever two of its three arguments are equal.
definition: A [nonassociative ring](c:nonassociative-ring) $R$ is alternative when $(x,x,y)=0$ and $(y,x,x)=0$ for all $x,y\in R$, where $(x,y,z)=(xy)z-x(yz)$. Equivalently, $x(xy)=(xx)y$ and $(yx)x=y(xx)$ for all $x,y\in R$.
examples: Every associative ring is alternative, because all its associators are zero.
The octonions form an alternative ring that is not associative: for suitable basis units $i,j,l$ one has $(ij)l=-i(jl)$.
Non-example: $\mathbb{R}^3$ with the cross product is not alternative, because $e_1\times(e_1\times e_2)=-e_2$ while $(e_1\times e_1)\times e_2=0$.

steps: An alternative ring has an addition and a product that is bilinear over the addition.
So it is a [nonassociative ring](c:nonassociative-ring), where associativity is not required.
The alternative case adds the identities $x(xy)=(xx)y$ and $(yx)x=y(xx)$.
links.why: It shows that alternative rings sit between associative rings and arbitrary nonassociative rings.

steps: Let $R$ be an associative [ring](c:ring).
Then $(xy)z=x(yz)$ for all $x,y,z$, so every associator $(x,y,z)$ is zero.
In particular $(x,x,y)=0$ and $(y,x,x)=0$, so $R$ is an alternative ring.
links.why: It shows that alternative rings include all associative rings.

steps: Take the [octonions](c:octonion) with their usual product.
Any two octonions generate an associative subalgebra, so $x(xy)=(xx)y$ and $(yx)x=y(xx)$ hold.
So the octonions are an alternative ring that is not associative.
links.why: It shows that alternative rings go beyond associative rings, with the octonions as the main example.

reminder: Betweenness is a relation on three points that holds when the middle point lies strictly between the other two on a line.
definition: In an incidence geometry, betweenness is a ternary [relation](c:relation) $B(a,b,c)$ on [points](c:point), read as \"$b$ lies strictly between $a$ and $c$\". It holds only for three distinct points on one [line](c:line), it is symmetric in $a$ and $c$, and for three points of a line it holds for exactly one choice of the middle point. For points of a real vector space, $B(a,b,c)$ means $b=(1-t)a+tc$ for some $0<t<1$.
examples: On the real line, $B(a,b,c)$ holds when $a<b<c$ or $c<b<a$.
In the plane, the midpoint $m$ of two distinct points $a$ and $c$ satisfies $B(a,m,c)$.
Non-example: if $a$, $b$ and $c$ do not lie on one line, then none of them lies between the other two.

reminder: A Carathéodory domain is a bounded simply connected plane domain whose boundary equals the boundary of the unbounded part of its complement.
definition: A Carathéodory domain is a bounded, [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space) domain $G\subset\mathbb{C}$ whose [boundary](c:boundary) equals the boundary of the unbounded component of $\mathbb{C}\setminus\overline{G}$. In other words, every boundary point of $G$ is also a limit of points of that unbounded component.
examples: Every Jordan domain, the inside of a simple closed curve, is a Carathéodory domain, for example a disc or a square.
Every bounded convex open set in the plane is a Carathéodory domain, because its boundary is a simple closed curve.
Non-example: the slit disc $\mathbb{D}\setminus[0,1)$ is not a Carathéodory domain, because its slit is part of its boundary, but it is not on the boundary of the outside of the closed disc.

reminder: A Cartan subgroup of a reductive group is the centralizer of a Cartan subalgebra.
definition: Let $G$ be a reductive [Lie group](c:lie-group) with Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$, and let $\mathfrak{h}$ be a [Cartan subalgebra](c:cartan-subalgebra) of $\mathfrak{g}$. The Cartan subgroup of $G$ attached to $\mathfrak{h}$ is $\{g\in G:\mathrm{Ad}(g)H=H\text{ for all }H\in\mathfrak{h}\}$. In a compact connected Lie group the Cartan subgroups are the [maximal tori](c:maximal-torus).
examples: In $GL_n(\mathbb{C})$, the group of invertible diagonal matrices is a Cartan subgroup.
In $SU(2)$, the group of matrices $\mathrm{diag}(e^{i\theta},e^{-i\theta})$ is a Cartan subgroup, and it is a maximal torus.
In $SL_2(\mathbb{R})$ there are two conjugacy classes of Cartan subgroups: the compact group $SO(2)$ and the group of real diagonal matrices of determinant $1$.
Non-example: in $GL_2(\mathbb{C})$, the upper triangular matrices form a Borel subgroup, which is not abelian, so it is not a Cartan subgroup.

steps: Let $G$ be a compact connected Lie group, and let $T$ be a [maximal torus](c:maximal-torus) with Lie algebra $\mathfrak{t}$.
Then $\mathfrak{t}$ is a Cartan subalgebra of $\mathfrak{g}$.
A maximal torus is its own centralizer in $G$, so the centralizer of $\mathfrak{t}$ is $T$.
So $T$ is a Cartan subgroup.
links.why: It shows that Cartan subgroups extend the idea of a maximal torus to noncompact groups.

reminder: A congruence subgroup of $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ is a subgroup that contains all matrices congruent to the identity modulo some $n$.
definition: For $n\ge1$, let $\Gamma(n)$ be the kernel of reduction modulo $n$ on the [special linear group](c:special-linear-group) $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$. A congruence subgroup is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ that contains $\Gamma(n)$ for some $n$, and the least such $n$ is its level.
examples: The group $\Gamma_0(N)$ of matrices in $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ with lower left entry divisible by $N$ is a congruence subgroup of level $N$.
The group $\Gamma_1(N)$, where also $a\equiv d\equiv1\pmod N$, and the group $\Gamma(N)$ itself are congruence subgroups of level $N$.
Non-example: the infinite cyclic subgroup generated by $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has infinite index, but every $\Gamma(n)$ has finite index, so it contains no $\Gamma(n)$.

steps: A congruence subgroup is a [subgroup](c:subgroup) of $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$.
It adds the condition that it contains $\Gamma(n)$ for some $n$, so it has finite index.
links.why: It shows that a congruence subgroup is a subgroup that is controlled by arithmetic modulo $n$.

steps: A congruence subgroup $\Gamma$ lies in $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$, which is a discrete subgroup of $SL_2(\mathbb{R})$.
So $\Gamma$ is discrete, and its image in $PSL_2(\mathbb{R})$ acts on the upper half-plane by Möbius maps.
Hence the image of $\Gamma$ is a [Fuchsian group](c:fuchsian-group).
The congruence case adds that $\Gamma$ contains some $\Gamma(n)$ and has finite index.
links.why: It shows that congruence subgroups give quotients of the upper half-plane, the modular curves.

reminder: A coring over a ring $A$ is an $A$-bimodule with a coassociative comultiplication and a counit, both $A$-bilinear.
definition: A coring over a [ring](c:ring) $A$ is an $A$-[bimodule](c:bimodule) $C$ with $A$-bimodule maps $\Delta:C\to C\otimes_AC$ and $\varepsilon:C\to A$ such that $\Delta$ is coassociative and $(\varepsilon\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta=\mathrm{id}=(\mathrm{id}\otimes\varepsilon)\Delta$. Equivalently, it is a [comonoid](c:comonoid) in the [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category) of $A$-bimodules with the tensor product $\otimes_A$.
examples: A coalgebra over a commutative ring $k$ is a coring over $A=k$.
For a ring extension $A\to B$, the module $B\otimes_AB$ is a coring over $B$, the Sweedler coring, with $\Delta(b\otimes b')=b\otimes1\otimes b'$ and $\varepsilon(b\otimes b')=bb'$.
Non-example: an algebra $A$ with its multiplication $A\otimes A\to A$ is not a coring, because the map goes in the wrong direction.

steps: Start with a [coalgebra](c:coalgebra) $C$ over a commutative ring $k$.
Take $A=k$, and let $k$ act in the same way on both sides of $C$.
Then $\otimes_k$ is $\otimes_A$, so $\Delta$ and $\varepsilon$ are $A$-bimodule maps.
So $C$ is a coring over $A=k$.
links.why: It shows that a coring is a coalgebra whose base ring may be noncommutative.

steps: Take the monoidal category of $A$-bimodules, with the tensor product $\otimes_A$ and the unit $A$.
A [comonoid](c:comonoid) in it is an object with a coassociative comultiplication and a counit.
That is exactly an $A$-coring.
links.why: It shows that a coring is a comonoid in one special monoidal category.

reminder: A curve of constant width is a convex curve with the same distance between parallel supporting lines in every direction.
definition: The width of a [convex curve](c:convex-curve) $C$ in a direction $u$ is the distance between the two parallel supporting lines of $C$ that are perpendicular to $u$. The curve $C$ has constant width $w$ when this distance equals $w$ for every direction $u$.
examples: A circle of diameter $w$ has constant width $w$.
The Reuleaux triangle, made of three circular arcs through the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side $w$, has constant width $w$.
Non-example: the ellipse $x^2/4+y^2=1$ has width $2$ in the $y$ direction and width $4$ in the $x$ direction, so its width is not constant.

steps: Let $C$ be a curve of constant width $w$, and let $K$ be the convex body that it bounds.
Then $C$ is the boundary of a convex set, so $C$ is a [convex curve](c:convex-curve).
The constant-width case adds that the width of $K$ in every direction equals $w$.
links.why: It shows that results about convex curves apply to curves of constant width, which add one condition.

reminder: A discrete series representation is an irreducible unitary representation whose matrix coefficients are square integrable.
definition: Let $G$ be a [locally compact group](c:locally-compact-group) with [Haar measure](c:haar-measure). A discrete series representation of $G$ is an [irreducible](c:irreducible-representation) [unitary representation](c:unitary-representation) $\pi$ whose matrix coefficients $g\mapsto\langle\pi(g)v,w\rangle$ are [square integrable](c:square-integrable-function) on $G$. For unimodular $G$, this means that $\pi$ is a closed subrepresentation of the regular representation on $L^2(G)$.
examples: Every irreducible unitary representation of a compact group is a discrete series representation, because its matrix coefficients are bounded and $G$ has finite measure.
For $SL_2(\mathbb{R})$ and each integer $k\ge2$, the holomorphic discrete series acts on the holomorphic functions $f$ on the upper half-plane with $\int|f|^2y^{k-2}\,dx\,dy<\infty$.
Non-example: the principal series representations of $SL_2(\mathbb{R})$ are irreducible and unitary, but their matrix coefficients are not square integrable.

steps: A discrete series representation of $G$ is first of all an irreducible [unitary representation](c:unitary-representation) on a Hilbert space.
It adds the condition that its matrix coefficients lie in $L^2(G)$.
So it is a unitary representation that also occurs discretely in the regular representation.
links.why: It shows that discrete series representations are the unitary representations that are square integrable.

reminder: A domain of holomorphy is an open set in $\mathbb{C}^n$ with a holomorphic function that has no holomorphic extension to any larger domain.
definition: An open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{C}^n$ is a domain of holomorphy when no nonempty open set $U\subseteq\Omega$ and connected open set $V\not\subseteq\Omega$ with $U\subseteq V\cap\Omega$ have the following property: every [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) on $\Omega$ agrees on $U$ with a holomorphic function on $V$. Equivalently, some holomorphic function on $\Omega$ has no [analytic continuation](c:analytic-continuation) across any boundary point of $\Omega$.
examples: Every open subset of $\mathbb{C}$ is a domain of holomorphy.
Every convex open subset of $\mathbb{C}^n$, such as a ball or a polydisc, is a domain of holomorphy.
Non-example: $\mathbb{C}^2\setminus\{0\}$ is not a domain of holomorphy, because every holomorphic function on it extends to $\mathbb{C}^2$ (Hartogs).

steps: Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{C}^n$ be a domain of holomorphy.
By the Cartan-Thullen theorem, $\Omega$ is holomorphically convex.
The coordinate functions are holomorphic on $\Omega$, so they separate points and give local coordinates.
So $\Omega$ is a [Stein manifold](c:stein-manifold).
links.why: It shows that domains of holomorphy in $\mathbb{C}^n$ are Stein manifolds, so Stein theory applies to them.

reminder: An exterior differential system on a manifold is an ideal of differential forms that is closed under the exterior derivative.
definition: An exterior differential system on a smooth [manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ is a differential ideal $\mathcal{I}$ of the algebra of [differential forms](c:differential-form) on $M$, that is, an ideal with $d\mathcal{I}\subseteq\mathcal{I}$. An integral manifold of $\mathcal{I}$ is a [submanifold](c:submanifold) $N\subseteq M$ on which every form of $\mathcal{I}$ restricts to zero.
examples: On $\mathbb{R}^3$, let $\theta=dz-y\,dx$. The ideal generated by $\theta$ and $d\theta$ is the contact system, and its integral curves are the Legendrian curves.
A first-order system $\dot x=F(x)$ gives the system on $\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}$ generated by $dx_i-F_i(x)\,dt$, and its integral curves are the graphs of solutions.
Non-example: on $\mathbb{R}^3$, the ideal generated by $\theta=dz-y\,dx$ alone is not an exterior differential system, because $d\theta=dx\wedge dy$ is not in it.

reminder: A module is faithfully flat when it is flat and its tensor product with any nonzero module is nonzero.
definition: A [module](c:module) $M$ over a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$ is faithfully flat when it is [flat](c:flat-module) and $M\otimes_RN\ne0$ for every nonzero $R$-module $N$. Equivalently, a sequence of $R$-modules is exact exactly when its [tensor product](c:tensor-product) with $M$ is exact.
examples: Every free module $R^n$ with $n\ge1$ is faithfully flat, and so is the polynomial ring $R[x]$ as an $R$-module.
Every field extension $L/K$ makes $L$ a faithfully flat $K$-module.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Q}$ is a flat $\mathbb{Z}$-module, but $\mathbb{Q}\otimes\mathbb{Z}/2=0$, so it is not faithfully flat.
Non-example: the zero module is flat, but it is not faithfully flat.

steps: Let $M$ be a faithfully flat $R$-module.
By definition $M$ is [flat](c:flat-module), so tensoring with $M$ keeps exact sequences exact.
Faithful flatness adds that $M\otimes N=0$ forces $N=0$.
links.why: It shows that faithfully flat modules are the flat modules that also detect exactness and vanishing.

reminder: A finite simple group is a nontrivial finite group whose only normal subgroups are the trivial group and the whole group.
definition: A [finite group](c:finite-group) $G\ne1$ is simple when its only [normal subgroups](c:normal-subgroup) are $1$ and $G$. By the classification, every finite simple group is cyclic of prime order, alternating of degree at least $5$, of Lie type, or one of the $26$ sporadic groups.
examples: The cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}/p$ is simple for every prime $p$.
The alternating group $A_n$ is simple for $n\ge5$, and $A_5$ of order $60$ is the smallest nonabelian simple group.
The Monster is a sporadic simple group.
Non-example: $A_4$ is not simple, because the Klein four-group is a normal subgroup.

steps: A [simple group](c:simple-group) is a nontrivial group with no normal subgroups other than $1$ and itself.
A finite simple group is such a group that is also finite.
So the finite case adds only that the group has finitely many elements.
links.why: It shows that finite simple groups are the finite ones among all simple groups.

steps: A finite simple group is a [finite group](c:finite-group).
It adds the condition that its only normal subgroups are $1$ and the group itself.
links.why: It shows that finite simple groups are the building blocks of finite groups.

reminder: An equilibrium is globally asymptotically stable when it is Lyapunov stable and every solution tends to it.
definition: An equilibrium $x^*$ of $\dot x=f(x)$ is globally asymptotically stable when it is [Lyapunov stable](c:lyapunov-stability) and $x(t)\to x^*$ as $t\to\infty$ for every solution $x$, whatever its initial value. Then $x^*$ is the only equilibrium of the system.
examples: The origin is globally asymptotically stable for $\dot x=-x$, because $x(t)=x(0)e^{-t}\to0$.
The origin is globally asymptotically stable for $\dot x=-x^3$ on $\mathbb{R}$.
Non-example: the origin of $\dot x=-x+x^3$ is asymptotically stable, but not globally, because solutions with $|x(0)|>1$ leave to infinity.
Non-example: the origin of $\ddot x=-x$ is Lyapunov stable, but solutions do not tend to it.

steps: Let $x^*$ be a globally asymptotically stable equilibrium.
By definition $x^*$ is [Lyapunov stable](c:lyapunov-stability).
The global asymptotic case adds that every solution converges to $x^*$ as $t\to\infty$.
links.why: It shows that global asymptotic stability is Lyapunov stability plus global convergence.

reminder: The Hilbert class field of a number field is its maximal unramified abelian extension.
definition: The Hilbert class field $H$ of a [number field](c:number-field) $K$ is the maximal [abelian extension](c:abelian-extension) of $K$ that is unramified at every place, the infinite places included. Its [Galois group](c:galois-group) over $K$ is isomorphic to the [ideal class group](c:ideal-class-group) of $K$ through the Artin map, so $[H:K]$ is the class number of $K$.
examples: For $K=\mathbb{Q}$, or any $K$ of class number $1$, the Hilbert class field is $K$ itself.
For $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-5})$, which has class number $2$, the Hilbert class field is $K(i)$.
For $K=\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-23})$, which has class number $3$, the Hilbert class field is $K(\alpha)$ with $\alpha^3-\alpha-1=0$.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ is an abelian extension of $\mathbb{Q}$, but it is ramified at $2$, so it does not lie in the Hilbert class field of $\mathbb{Q}$.

steps: Let $H$ be the Hilbert class field of $K$.
By definition $H/K$ is Galois with an abelian Galois group, so it is an [abelian extension](c:abelian-extension).
The Hilbert class field adds that no prime of $K$ ramifies in $H$, and that $H$ is the largest such extension.
links.why: It shows that the Hilbert class field is the largest abelian extension without ramification.

reminder: Hilbert's axioms are a list of axioms for Euclidean geometry in five groups: incidence, order, congruence, parallels and continuity.
definition: Hilbert's axioms describe Euclidean geometry with the primitive objects point, line and plane, and the primitive relations of incidence, [betweenness](c:betweenness) and [congruence](c:congruence-in-geometry). The axioms fall into five groups: incidence, order, congruence, the parallel axiom, and continuity, which holds the Archimedean axiom and the completeness axiom.
examples: An incidence axiom: two distinct points lie on exactly one line.
An order axiom, Pasch's axiom: a line that meets one side of a triangle and passes through no vertex also meets another side.
The parallel axiom: through a point outside a line passes at most one line that does not meet the first line.
Non-example: the Crossbar theorem is not one of Hilbert's axioms, because it is proved from them.

reminder: Every map factors as a surjection onto its image followed by an injection of the image into the codomain.
definition: An image factorization of a map $f:X\to Y$ is a way to write $f=m\circ e$, where $e:X\to I$ is a [surjection](c:surjection) and $m:I\to Y$ is an [injection](c:injection). Then $I$ is the [image](c:image) of $f$. In a category the same holds with an epimorphism and a monomorphism, and $m$ is the smallest subobject of $Y$ through which $f$ factors.
examples: The map $x\mapsto x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$ factors as the surjection $\mathbb{R}\to[0,\infty)$ followed by the inclusion into $\mathbb{R}$.
A group homomorphism $f:G\to H$ factors as $G\to G/\ker f\cong f(G)\hookrightarrow H$.
A continuous map factors through its image with the subspace topology, and the map is an embedding exactly when the surjection is a homeomorphism.
Non-example: the constant map $\{0,1\}\to\{0\}$ equals $\{0,1\}\hookrightarrow\{0,1,2\}\to\{0\}$, but this puts the injection first, and its middle set is larger than the image.

reminder: An $L^1$ contraction is a linear operator on $L^1$ that does not increase the $L^1$ norm.
definition: A linear operator $T:L^1(\mu)\to L^1(\mu)$ on a [measure space](c:measure-space) is an $L^1$ contraction when $\|Tf\|_1\le\|f\|_1$ for every $f\in L^1(\mu)$. In other words, its [operator norm](c:operator-norm) on the [integrable functions](c:l1-space) is at most $1$.
examples: The identity operator is an $L^1$ contraction.
For a measure-preserving map $\tau$, the operator $f\mapsto f\circ\tau$ is an $L^1$ contraction.
For a probability space, conditional expectation $f\mapsto\mathbb{E}[f\mid\mathcal{G}]$ onto a sub-sigma-algebra is an $L^1$ contraction.
Non-example: the operator $f\mapsto2f$ is not an $L^1$ contraction, because it doubles the norm.

steps: Let $T$ be an $L^1$ contraction on $L^1(\mu)$.
Then $\|Tf\|_1\le\|f\|_1$, so $T$ is a [bounded linear operator](c:bounded-linear-operator) with norm at most $1$.
The contraction case adds that the bound on the norm is $1$.
links.why: It shows that contractions are the bounded operators with norm at most one, which iterate without growth.

reminder: Mod $p$ homology is homology with coefficients in the field of integers modulo a prime $p$.
definition: For a prime $p$ and a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$, the mod $p$ homology $H_n(X;\mathbb{F}_p)$ is the [homology](c:homology) of the chain complex $C_\bullet(X)\otimes\mathbb{F}_p$, where $C_\bullet(X)$ is the singular chain complex and $\mathbb{F}_p=\mathbb{Z}/p$ is the [prime field](c:prime-field). Each $H_n(X;\mathbb{F}_p)$ is an $\mathbb{F}_p$-vector space, and $H_n(X;\mathbb{F}_p)\cong H_n(X)\otimes\mathbb{F}_p\oplus\mathrm{Tor}(H_{n-1}(X),\mathbb{F}_p)$.
examples: For a sphere $S^m$ with $m\ge1$, $H_n(S^m;\mathbb{F}_p)$ is $\mathbb{F}_p$ for $n=0$ and $n=m$, and $0$ otherwise.
For the real projective plane, $H_n(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{F}_2)=\mathbb{F}_2$ for $n=0,1,2$, but $H_n(\mathbb{RP}^2;\mathbb{F}_3)=0$ for $n>0$.
Non-example: the integral group $H_1(S^1;\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}$ is not a mod $p$ homology group, because it is not a vector space over $\mathbb{F}_p$.

steps: Homology with coefficients in an abelian group $A$ is the [homology](c:homology) of the chain complex $C_\bullet(X)\otimes A$.
Choose $A=\mathbb{F}_p=\mathbb{Z}/p$.
The result is mod $p$ homology.
links.why: It shows that mod $p$ homology is ordinary homology with one choice of coefficients, so its tools carry over.

reminder: A line bundle on a projective variety is nef when its degree on every curve is nonnegative.
definition: A [line bundle](c:line-bundle) $L$ on a [projective variety](c:projective-variety) $X$ is nef when $L\cdot C\ge0$ for every irreducible [curve](c:curve) $C\subseteq X$. Here $L\cdot C=\deg(L|_C)$ is the [intersection number](c:intersection-number) of $L$ with $C$.
examples: The trivial bundle $\mathcal{O}_X$ is nef, because it has degree $0$ on every curve.
Every globally generated line bundle is nef, because for each curve some section does not vanish on it, which gives degree at least $0$.
Every ample line bundle is nef, and it even has positive degree on every curve.
Non-example: $\mathcal{O}(-1)$ on $\mathbb{P}^1$ has degree $-1$ on $\mathbb{P}^1$ itself, so it is not nef.

steps: Let $L$ be an [ample line bundle](c:ample-sheaf) on a projective variety $X$.
Some power $L^m$ is very ample, so it embeds $X$ in projective space.
For every curve $C$, the number $L^m\cdot C$ is the degree of the embedded curve, which is positive.
So $L\cdot C=\tfrac1m L^m\cdot C>0$ for every curve $C$, and $L$ is nef.
links.why: It shows that nefness is the closed version of ampleness: the strict inequality becomes a weak one.

reminder: The Petrov classification sorts the Weyl tensor of a four-dimensional spacetime by how many of its principal null directions coincide.
definition: At a point of a four-dimensional [Lorentzian manifold](c:lorentzian-manifold), the [Weyl tensor](c:weyl-tensor) has four principal null directions, counted with multiplicity. The Petrov classification sorts the Weyl tensor into types I (four distinct directions), II (one repeated pair), D (two repeated pairs), III (one triple direction), N (one quadruple direction) and O (the Weyl tensor is zero).
examples: The Schwarzschild [spacetime](c:spacetime) has Petrov type D.
A plane gravitational wave has Petrov type N.
Minkowski space and the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker spacetimes are conformally flat, so they have Petrov type O.
Non-example: the Segre classification, not the Petrov classification, sorts the Ricci tensor, because the Petrov classification uses only the Weyl tensor.

reminder: A piecewise-linear manifold is a manifold with an atlas whose transition maps are piecewise linear.
definition: A piecewise-linear manifold of dimension $n$ is a [manifold](c:manifold) with an atlas of charts to open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ whose transition maps are piecewise linear [homeomorphisms](c:homeomorphism). Equivalently, it is a space with a triangulation in which the link of every vertex is a piecewise-linear sphere or ball.
examples: The boundary of an $(n+1)$-simplex is a piecewise-linear $n$-sphere.
Every smooth manifold has a piecewise-linear structure, by smooth triangulation (Whitehead).
Non-example: Freedman's $E_8$ manifold has no piecewise-linear structure, because in dimension $4$ such a structure gives a smooth structure and this manifold has none.

steps: Let $M$ be a piecewise-linear manifold, with an atlas whose transition maps are piecewise linear.
Piecewise linear homeomorphisms are homeomorphisms, so the same atlas makes $M$ a topological [manifold](c:manifold).
The piecewise-linear case adds that all transition maps are piecewise linear.
links.why: It shows that a piecewise-linear manifold is a manifold with extra structure on its charts.

reminder: A pluripolar set is a set that lies locally inside the $-\infty$ set of a plurisubharmonic function.
definition: A subset $E$ of a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) $X$ is pluripolar when every point of $X$ has an [open neighbourhood](c:open-neighbourhood) $U$ and a plurisubharmonic function $\varphi\not\equiv-\infty$ on $U$ with $E\cap U\subseteq\{\varphi=-\infty\}$. By Josefson’s theorem, for $X=\mathbb{C}^n$ one plurisubharmonic function on the whole space then works for $E$.
examples: The zero set $\{f=0\}$ of a holomorphic function $f\not\equiv0$ is pluripolar, with $\varphi=\log|f|$.
Every countable union of pluripolar sets in $\mathbb{C}^n$ is pluripolar.
Non-example: $\mathbb{R}^n\subset\mathbb{C}^n$ is not pluripolar, and neither is any set with nonempty interior.

steps: Let $E$ be pluripolar, so locally $E\subseteq\{\varphi=-\infty\}$ for a plurisubharmonic function $\varphi\not\equiv-\infty$.
Such a function is locally integrable, so the set where $\varphi=-\infty$ has Lebesgue measure zero.
So every point has a neighbourhood in which $E$ has [measure zero](c:measure-zero), and $E$ has measure zero.
The pluripolar case adds that $E$ is also small in the sense of complex analysis.
links.why: It shows that pluripolar sets are negligible for integration, and that they are much smaller than general null sets.

reminder: A principal torus bundle is a principal bundle whose structure group is a torus.
definition: A principal torus bundle is a [principal bundle](c:principal-bundle) $\pi:P\to B$ whose structure group is a [torus](c:torus) $T^n=(S^1)^n$. The torus acts freely on $P$, and it acts transitively on each fibre of $\pi$.
examples: The Hopf fibration $S^3\to S^2$ is a principal bundle for the circle $T^1$.
The product $B\times T^n\to B$ is the trivial principal $T^n$-bundle.
Over a nice space $B$, principal $T^n$-bundles correspond to classes in $H^2(B;\mathbb{Z}^n)$, their Chern classes.
Non-example: the Klein bottle fibres over the circle with circle fibres, but it is not a principal circle bundle, because the monodromy is a reflection and not a rotation.

steps: A [principal bundle](c:principal-bundle) has a structure group $G$ that acts freely and transitively on the fibres.
Choose $G=T^n=(S^1)^n$, a torus.
The result is a principal torus bundle.
links.why: It shows that general theory of principal bundles, such as classifying spaces, applies to torus bundles.

reminder: A punctured neighbourhood of a point is a neighbourhood of that point with the point itself removed.
definition: Let $x$ be a point of a [topological space](c:topological-space). A punctured neighbourhood of $x$ is a set $U\setminus\{x\}$, where $U$ is a [neighbourhood](c:neighborhood) of $x$, and often $U$ is also required to be open.
examples: In $\mathbb{R}$, the set $(x-\varepsilon,x)\cup(x,x+\varepsilon)$ with $\varepsilon>0$ is a punctured neighbourhood of $x$.
In $\mathbb{C}$, the punctured disc $\{z:0<|z-a|<r\}$ is a punctured neighbourhood of $a$.
Non-example: the set $(x,x+\varepsilon)$ is not a punctured neighbourhood of $x$ in $\mathbb{R}$, because $[x,x+\varepsilon)$ is not a neighbourhood of $x$.

reminder: A Pythagorean field is a field in which the sum of two squares is again a square.
definition: A [field](c:field) $F$ is Pythagorean when for all $a,b\in F$ there is $c\in F$ with $a^2+b^2=c^2$. Then every finite sum of squares in $F$ is a square.
examples: The real numbers form a Pythagorean field, and so do the complex numbers, in which every element is a square.
The field of constructible real numbers is Pythagorean, because $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ is constructible when $a$ and $b$ are.
Non-example: the rational numbers are not Pythagorean, because $1^2+1^2=2$ is not a square in $\mathbb{Q}$.

steps: A Pythagorean field is first of all a [field](c:field).
It adds the condition that $a^2+b^2$ is a square for all $a$ and $b$.
links.why: It shows that Pythagorean fields are the fields where the Pythagorean theorem needs no new numbers.

steps: Let $F$ be a [Euclidean field](c:euclidean-field): an ordered field in which every positive element is a square.
For $a,b\in F$, the sum $a^2+b^2$ is nonnegative, so it is a square $c^2$ in $F$.
So $F$ is a Pythagorean field, and the Euclidean case adds an ordering in which the squares are exactly the nonnegative elements.
links.why: It shows that every Euclidean field is Pythagorean, but not the other way around.

reminder: A real quadratic field is a number field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d)$ with $d>1$ a squarefree integer.
definition: A real quadratic field is a [number field](c:number-field) of degree $2$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ that lies in $\mathbb{R}$. Each one is $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d)=\{a+b\sqrt d:a,b\in\mathbb{Q}\}$ for a unique squarefree integer $d>1$.
examples: The fields $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)$ and $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt3)$ are real quadratic fields.
The field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt5)$ is a real quadratic field, and the golden ratio $(1+\sqrt5)/2$ is a [fundamental unit](c:fundamental-unit) of its ring of integers.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Q}(i)$ has degree $2$, but it is not contained in $\mathbb{R}$, so it is imaginary quadratic.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{2})$ lies in $\mathbb{R}$, but it has degree $3$.

steps: A real quadratic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d)$ is a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ of degree $2$.
Every finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ is a [number field](c:number-field).
The real quadratic case adds that the degree is $2$ and the field lies in $\mathbb{R}$.
links.why: It shows that general results on number fields apply to $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt d)$, which has a simple explicit form.

reminder: Risk is the uncertainty of a payoff that is modelled by a random variable with a known distribution.
definition: Risk is the uncertainty of a payoff that is described by a [random variable](c:random-variable) $X$ with a known [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution). A risk-averse person, with a [concave](c:concave-function) utility $u$, values $X$ below its [expected value](c:expected-value); the gap $\mathbb{E}[X]-u^{-1}(\mathbb{E}[u(X)])$ is the risk premium.
examples: A bet that pays $100$ or $0$ with probability $\tfrac12$ each is risky, and its expected value is $50$.
A sure payoff of $50$ carries no risk, because a constant random variable has variance zero.
Non-example: a situation whose probabilities are unknown is Knightian uncertainty, not risk in this sense.
